title: Bowen says 'no carve-outs' after Queensland claims data centre win

Topic:Federal Government

Chris Bowen has slapped down Queensland and the Northern Territory, insisting they have not been given a carve-out from new data centre rules. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Energy Minister Chris Bowen has rejected claims Queensland and the Northern Territory secured a carve-out from new rules requiring data centres to use 100 per cent renewables.

States will be able to seek approval to use alternatives like coal or gas, but Mr Bowen says the Commonwealth will have the final say and the threshold will be "very high".

The federal government will release draft national data centre standards before seeking to pass the legislation early next year.

Queensland and the Northern Territory will not have control over how data centres are powered, the federal government insists, declaring there will be "no exceptions and no carve-outs" under its renewables plan.

Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen told the ABC the national standards governing the development of data centres in Australia would still require them to bring their own "100 per cent" renewable energy plus firming through battery storage or gas.

Mr Bowen has rejected claims this element of the Commonwealth's plan was watered down after a meeting of national cabinet on Wednesday where Queensland Premier David Crisafulli claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered.

"So, as we said we would, we are legislating nationally consistent standards across the board with no exceptions and no carve-outs," Mr Bowen said.

Australia’s appeal as a destination for data centres has given it bargaining power in the AI boom.

"The only change is that where a state owned government electricity company asserts that they can do it cheaper than renewables, they can apply to the Commonwealth to do that."

In response, the Queensland government has now argued Mr Bowen's "rhetoric" was not contributing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's "goal" of proving a "positive path forward" on data centres.

Premiers and chief ministers signed off on new data centre standards requiring data centre operators to invest in new renewable energy to offset their power usage, but also gave flexibility for state-owned electricity assets.

This was widely interpreted as a capitulation to Queensland and the Northern Territory, which had both insisted they would not be dictated to by Canberra.

Mr Bowen said it would be up to the Commonwealth to "decide" whether to let states use coal or gas as a main power source, and they would have to prove it was "cheaper and better for the grid than renewables would be".

"[That] is a very high bar and very difficult to do, but some states may choose to do that," he said.

Mr Bowen said the Australian Energy Regulator (AER), on behalf of the Commonwealth, would consider states' applications and "make a decision".

"But we will be legislating those standards, which will apply equally in Queensland and the Northern Territory as everywhere else," he said.

"I think it would be very, very difficult indeed for a state energy company to establish to the Commonwealth's satisfaction that a coal arrangement will be cheaper than renewables."

David Crisafulli had claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

In a statement on Friday, Queensland Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki said the purpose of the national data centre standards was to provide a "positive path forward and certainty for Australians, government and industry".

"Chris Bowen's rhetoric is not contributing to that goal," he said.

"The Queensland government will remain focused on the decisions made by national cabinet — acknowledging Queensland's unique position in owning generation and distribution assets and the energy mix that comes with that."

Mr Janetzki said his government was "grateful for the maturity and pragmatism" shown by Mr Albanese.

Following Wednesday's national cabinet meeting, Mr Crisafulli had told the ABC his state had been given a carve-out from the renewables policy.

"It's a big win, not just for our economy, it's a big win for people's power bills as well," he said.

"Because we own our assets, our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board.

"That new energy opportunity can be the abundance of gas we have, the surplus coal-fired power generation we have in the system, it can be renewable energy opportunities."

But Mr Bowen said on Friday it was "not accurate" for states or territories to say they would be able to make the decision about how data centres were powered.

"I do understand the confusion, but the Commonwealth will decide this because it's Commonwealth law," he said.

As is so often the case in Australia, the politics came down to a fight over energy.

"Gas and coal are not generally cheaper than renewables, but if a state-owned energy company wants to claim that they are and get the Commonwealth figures to prove [it], then the AER will assess it.

Asked why he had picked a fight to force states to use renewables if he was always confident they would be the cheapest energy option, Mr Bowen said the impact on bills of an "alternative approach" was "too serious to risk".

"We know that if it was an open slather approach in Queensland, bills will be 13 per cent higher on a wholesale level," he said.

"We're not prepared to let ideology of the state government that might be anti-renewables lead to that poor outcome for consumers."

Mr Bowen said data centres were "electricity whales" that "eat" energy.

"So the implications of getting it wrong are too big to let the Commonwealth let a race to the bottom unfurl," he said.

Mr Bowen said the federal government would bring forward a "wholistic" piece of draft bill on data centres "in due course" ahead of passing legislation early next year.

He said his component of the bill would be based on the corporations powers in the constitution, which was "pretty clear" Commonwealth laws prevailed in any "dispute" with states.

"[It] will require registration of a data centre, which will require the use of renewable energy certificates to establish 100 per cent renewables backed by gas firming," he said.
